lesson.title: Use one query to define another

lead.text: The inner query runs first and passes its answer to the outer query. That answer can be a value or a set of ids.
EXISTS asks only whether the inner query returns any row at all.

steps.headline: A subquery is a query in brackets that supplies a value or a set to the outer query.

lead.text: The outer condition needs a number to compare with, and the subquery works it out first. One amount is unknown.

reveal.text: You compared each amount with the average the subquery found. An amount equal to it would not pass a strict comparison.

queries.label: Above the average
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount > (SELECT AVG(amount) FROM orders) ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Strictly above 80
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount > 80 ORDER BY id;

lead.text: IN keeps a row when its value is in the set the subquery returns. The outer result still has one row per order.

reveal.text: You found the customers first and then their orders. An order with an unknown amount still counts: IN looks at the customer.

queries.label: North customers' orders
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id, amount FROM orders WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT id FROM customers WHERE region = 'North') ORDER BY id;

queries.label: South customers' orders
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id, amount FROM orders WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT id FROM customers WHERE region = 'South') ORDER BY id;

steps.headline: Which customers have at least one order?

queries.label: At least one order
queries.sql: SELECT c.id, c.name FROM customers AS c WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders AS o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id) ORDER BY c.id;

queries.label: No orders
queries.sql: SELECT c.id, c.name FROM customers AS c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders AS o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id) ORDER BY c.id;

workedSteps.text: Take one customer at a time.
Ask the inner query whether any order has customer_id = 1.
NOT EXISTS keeps the customer whose inner query finds nothing.

lead.text: A subquery that refers to a value from the current outer row is called correlated. Its answer can change from one outer row to the next.

queries.label: Above overall average
queries.sql: SELECT id, item, amount FROM orders WHERE amount > (SELECT AVG(amount) FROM orders) ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Above its item average
queries.sql: SELECT o.id, o.item, o.amount FROM orders AS o WHERE o.amount > (SELECT AVG(i.amount) FROM orders AS i WHERE i.item = o.item) ORDER BY o.id;

lesson.orientation: Use scalar subqueries, IN and EXISTS without multiplying the outer result.
lesson.reviewLabel: Use one query to define another
lesson.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: Six pupils score 10, 50, 60, 70, 80 and 90. Everyone above the class average gets a sticker.

intro.promise: By the end you'll use a query inside a query to compare, to test membership and to check existence.

recap.keyIdea: A subquery supplies a value or a set to an outer query. EXISTS tests for a match without multiplying the outer rows.

blocks.text: You gave 3 stickers above an average of 60, then counted 4 orders from North customers. No order sits strictly above its own item's average.

recap.nextHook: Next, stack two results with UNION.

questions.prompt: How many orders have an amount greater than AVG(amount) over all orders?
hints: Calculate the average of known amounts.
Use a strict greater-than comparison.
The threshold is 240 ÷ 5; test each known amount against it.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The known average is 48; orders 101 and 103 each have amount 80.

questions.onCorrect: 2. The subquery gives the average, and only the amounts above it pass.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts every known amount. Only those above the average pass.
Check each known amount against the average. More than one is above it.

questions.prompt: How many orders belong to customers in the North region?
hints: Find customer ids in North first.
Count their orders even when an amount is missing.
North's customer ids are 1 and 3; each contributes two orders.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Customers 1 and 3 are North; each has two orders.

questions.onCorrect: 4. The subquery lists the North ids, and IN keeps every order that points at one of them.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the customers. Count the orders they placed.
That is every order. Only North customers count.
That drops an order because its amount is unknown. IN looks at the customer, not the amount.

questions.prompt: Why does EXISTS return Ada once even though she has two orders?
hints: It tests existence without adding each matching subquery row to the outer result.

acceptedIdeas: The outer query has one row per customer
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: EXISTS asks whether any matching order exists for each outer customer row. It does not create one outer row per match, so Ada appears once.

choices.label: The outer query has one row per customer

questions.onCorrect: The outer query has one row per customer. EXISTS only tests whether a match is there.

misconceptions.feedback: EXISTS never deletes anything. It only tests.
It does not skip rows. It only asks whether any row exists.

questions.prompt: How many orders are strictly above the average for their own item?
hints: Compare within each item group.
Equality does not pass a strict greater-than condition.
Each known amount equals its item's mean. Test whether equality satisfies a strict > comparison.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Desk amounts equal 80, Book amounts equal 20 and Lamp's known amount equals 40; each equals its item average.

questions.onCorrect: 0. Each known amount equals its item's average, and equal is not above.

misconceptions.feedback: Those are above the overall average. Each is only equal to its own item's average.

questions.prompt: Three customers have zero, one and four orders. How many customers pass EXISTS for an order?
hints: EXISTS asks whether there is at least one match.
Count customers with a nonzero number of orders.
Mark each customer whose order count is positive, then count marked customers once.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two customers have at least one order; the number of matches does not duplicate them.

questions.onCorrect: 2. EXISTS needs at least one order, and it counts each customer once.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the customer with no orders. EXISTS needs at least one match.
That adds up the orders. EXISTS counts customers, once each.

questions.prompt: What is the term for a subquery that refers to a value from the current outer row?
hints: Its condition depends on which row the outer query is considering.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A correlated subquery uses a value from the current outer row. Its meaning depends on which outer row is being considered.

questions.onCorrect: correlated. Its condition depends on the outer row, so it is run for each of them.

misconceptions.feedback: Nested only says where it sits. The word wanted describes how it uses the outer row.
Scalar describes a single value coming back. The word wanted is about depending on the outer row.

questions.prompt: How many pupils get a sticker?
hints: Find the class average first.
Add the scores and divide by how many there are.
Count the scores above that average, not equal to it.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The scores add up to 360, so the average is 60. The scores above it are 70, 80 and 90.

questions.onCorrect: 3. You worked out one value first and then compared every score with it. A subquery does the same inside a query.

misconceptions.feedback: A score equal to the average is not above it.

questions.prompt: What does the subquery in WHERE amount > (SELECT AVG(amount) FROM orders) supply?
hints: How many numbers does AVG return?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: AVG returns a single number, and the outer condition compares each amount with it.

questions.onCorrect: A subquery in parentheses can supply a value or a set to the outer query. Here it supplies one number.

misconceptions.feedback: Here the subquery returns a single number, not rows to join.
A subquery supplies values, not column names.

questions.prompt: Five customers have 0, 2, 0, 0 and 5 orders. How many customers pass NOT EXISTS for an order?
hints: NOT EXISTS keeps a customer when the inner query finds no order.
Which customers have no order at all?
Count the customers with zero orders.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three customers have no order, so NOT EXISTS keeps three.

questions.onCorrect: 3. NOT EXISTS keeps a customer exactly when the inner query finds nothing for them.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the customers who have orders. NOT EXISTS keeps those with none.
